analysis.one_liner: Bans PAC money in federal elections, restricts soft money, strengthens disclosure and FEC enforcement, and limits union political dues.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 1997, sent to four House committees and three subcommittees, drew no cosponsors, and died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overhauled how federal campaigns are financed. It would ban political action committees from spending in federal elections, bar national party committees from spending unregulated 'soft money' on federal races, cap how much a congressional candidate can raise from people outside their district or state, force disclosure of big 'bundled' donations and soft-money spending, and give the Federal Election Commission power to audit campaigns and go to court on its own. It would also stop candidates from using taxpayer-funded franked mass mailings. Separately, it would require workers in unionized workplaces to sign a written consent each year before any of their dues could go to politics beyond core bargaining activities.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, voters would see who is paying for campaign messages, since bundlers, soft-money spenders, and advertisers would have to identify themselves. Challengers would face incumbents who can no longer blanket districts with free taxpayer-funded mail or lean on PAC money, and candidates would need to raise most of their money from people who can actually vote for them. Employees required to pay union dues as a condition of employment would gain an annual, written opt-in before dues fund political activity.

how_it_helps.text: Bans political action committees from making contributions, soliciting funds, or spending to influence federal elections [S2][S3].
Prohibits national party committees from spending non-Federal 'soft money' on federal elections [S2][S3].
Caps out-of-district and out-of-state contributions at 40 percent of what a House or Senate candidate raises [S2][S3].
Treats checks routed through 'bundlers' as contributions from the bundler, and requires 48-hour disclosure of soft-money election spending above $2,000 by any person [S2][S3].
Lets the FEC conduct random audits, seek court injunctions when a violation is occurring or imminent, and litigate on its own behalf in court [S2][S3].
Bans Members of Congress from sending unsolicited mass mailings at taxpayer expense, a practice that gives incumbents a free re-election tool [S2][S3].

Requires workers to sign a written agreement, renewed annually, before unions may spend their dues on politics beyond collective bargaining, and requires unions to disclose spending by function [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporate, trade-association, and union PACs would lose their channel for funding federal campaigns. National party committees would lose soft money for federal races. Labor unions would face new consent and disclosure burdens on political dues. Incumbent members of Congress would lose franked mass mailings and would have to raise a majority of their money from constituents.

drawbacks.text: Banning PACs without a broader rewrite could push money into less accountable channels — individual checks routed through parties, independent groups, or state-level soft money — rather than reducing the total money in politics; the bill itself anticipates this by capping PAC contributions at $1,000 during any period the ban is not in effect [S3].

The dues-consent provisions weaken organized labor's capacity to fund politics, and their practical effect depends on unions themselves calculating and disclosing how much of each dues dollar goes to politics; labor organizations opposed this kind of 'paycheck protection' legislation as designed to hobble union political spending while leaving corporate political spending largely untouched (a widely reported objection of the era, not found in the provided sources).

Limits on out-of-district contributions could disadvantage challengers and parties in financially lopsided races, and expanding FEC audit and injunction powers concentrates enforcement discretion in a six-member commission.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The campaign-finance titles are a serious, broad anti-corruption package: a PAC ban, a soft-money restriction, bundler disclosure, and stronger FEC enforcement together attack the main channels through which organized money reaches federal campaigns. The offsetting costs are real but speculative — money may find other channels. The union-dues title is the bill's sharpest edge: it is framed as worker protection and does give individual workers consent rights, but its net effect is to shrink the political resources of one side of the political-money equation. The bill's fatal practical weakness was structural: sending it to four committees with no deadline gave no committee an incentive to act.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in four House committees after a simultaneous multi-committee referral, went to three subcommittees in the first month, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rob Portman (R-OH) introduced the bill on April 10, 1997 [S1][S5].

The House referred it the same day to four committees — Oversight, Education and the Workforce, Government Reform and Oversight, and Judiciary — 'for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker' [S3][S5].

In April and May 1997 it was referred to the Oversight Subcommittee on Postal Service, the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, and the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime [S5].
No committee reported the bill and no vote was ever taken; that was the last action recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs, national party committees raising soft money, and labor unions kept the campaign-money channels the bill would have closed, and incumbent members kept their franked mass mailings. Ordinary voters gained nothing: the disclosure and enforcement changes never took effect.

for.name: Rep. Rob Portman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on April 10, 1997.

against.name: House Oversight Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Postal Service Subcommittee and never brought it to a markup or vote.

against.name: Speaker of the House
against.role: Assigned the bill to four committees simultaneously
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to Oversight, Education and the Workforce, Government Reform and Oversight, and Judiciary at once, with a jurisdiction period left 'to be subsequently determined' and never determined.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees on Employer-Employee Relations and Crime; neither committee took it up.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and its sole sponsor was a Republican with no cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no partisan alignment on either side.

industries.note: Title V would require annual written consent before dues could fund politics beyond bargaining and would force detailed spending disclosure, shrinking union political treasuries. Unions argue dues-funded politics benefits their members collectively; the bill's answer is that individual workers should opt in.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, trade, and union PACs)
industries.note: The bill eliminates PACs as a vehicle for federal campaign money, ending their privileged, regulated access to lawmakers. Their interest in the status quo rests on money's continued role in campaigns, which runs against voters' interest in limiting it.

Parties would be barred from spending unregulated soft money on federal elections and would have to disclose issue and voter-drive spending above $2,000. Both major parties depended on soft money in the 1990s, so the bill curbs a revenue stream both guarded.

The bill strips incumbents of franked mass mailings, a free campaign communication funded by taxpayers, and restricts contributions from people who cannot vote for them. The bill's competitive-benefits flow to challengers at incumbent expense.
